entries.b324e126074bcc985497385828c70faf3f590c6e: <div sID="gen12059" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="89" osisID="Ps.89" sID="Ps.89"/> <div eID="gen12059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12060" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12061" type="x-p"/> Many psalms that begin with complaint and prayer end with joy and praise, but this begins with joy and praise and ends with sad complaints and petitions; for the psalmist first recounts God's former favours, and then with the consideration of them aggravates the present grievances. It is uncertain when it was penned; only, in general, that it was at a time when the house of David was woefully eclipsed; some think it was at the time of the captivity of Babylon, when king Zedekiah was insulted over, and abused, by Nebuchadnezzar, and then they make the title to signify no more than that the psalm was set to the tune of a song of Ethan the son of Zerah, called Maschil; others suppose it to be penned by Ethan, who is mentioned in the story of Solomon, who, outliving that glorious prince, thus lamented the great disgrace done to the house of David in the next reign by the revolt of the ten tribes. I. The psalmist, in the joyful pleasant part of the psalm, gives glory to God, and takes comfort to himself and his friends. This he does more briefly, mentioning God's mercy and truth (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.1">ver. 1</reference>) and his covenant (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.2-Ps.89.4">ver. 2-4</reference>), but more largely in the following verses, wherein, 1. He adores the glory and perfection of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.5-Ps.89.14">ver. 5-14</reference>. 2. He pleases himself in the happiness of those that are admitted into communion with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.15-Ps.89.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. 3. He builds all his hope upon God's covenant with David, as a type of Christ, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.19-Ps.89.37">ver. 19-37</reference>. II. In the melancholy part of the psalm he laments the present calamitous state of the prince and royal family (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.38-Ps.89.45">ver. 38-45</reference>), expostulates with God upon it (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.46-Ps.89.49">ver. 46-49</reference>), and then concludes with prayer for redress, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.50-Ps.89.51">ver. 50, 51</reference>. In singing this psalm we must have high thoughts of God, a lively faith in his covenant with the Redeemer, and a sympathy with the afflicted parts of the church.
entries.00647d762b8b49642864e5dd32641e5ed51c931b: <div eID="gen12061" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12060" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Mercy and Faithfulness.</title> <div sID="gen12062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will sing of the mercies of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. <hi type="super">2</hi> For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens. <hi type="super">3</hi> I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, <hi type="super">4</hi> Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah. <div eID="gen12062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12063" type="x-p"/> The psalmist has a very sad complaint to make of the deplorable condition of the family of David at this time, and yet he begins the psalm with songs of praise; for we must, in every thing, in every state, give thanks; thus we must glorify the Lord in the fire. We think, when we are in trouble, that we get ease by complaining; but we do more—we get joy, by praising. Let our complaints therefore be turned into thanksgivings; and in these verses we find that which will be matter of praise and thanksgiving for us in the worst of times, whether upon a personal or a public account, 1. However it be, the everlasting God is good and true, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.1">v. 1</reference>. Though we may find it hard to reconcile present dark providences with the goodness and truth of God, yet we must abide by this principle, That God's mercies are inexhaustible and his truth is inviolable; and these must be the matter of our joy and praise: "<hi type="italic">I will sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever,</hi> sing a praising song to God's honour, a pleasant song for my own solace, and <hi type="italic">Maschil,</hi> an instructive song, for the edification of others." We may be for ever singing God's mercies, and yet the subject will not be drawn dry. We must sing of God's mercies as long as we live, train up others to sing of them when we are gone, and hope to be singing them in heaven world without end; and this is <hi type="italic">singing of the mercies of the Lord for ever. With my mouth,</hi> and with my pen (for by that also do we speak), <hi type="italic">will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations,</hi> assuring posterity, from my own observation and experience, that God is true to every word that he has spoken, that they may learn to <hi type="italic">put their trust in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.6">Ps. lxxviii. 6</reference>. 2. However it be, the everlasting covenant is firm and sure, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.2-Ps.89.4">v. 2-4</reference>. Here we have, (1.) The psalmist's faith and hope: "Things now look black, and threaten the utter extirpation of the house of David; but <hi type="italic">I have said,</hi> and I have warrant from the word of God to say it, that <hi type="italic">mercy shall be built up for ever.</hi>" As the goodness of God's nature is to be the matter of our song (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.1">v. 1</reference>), so much more the mercy that is built for us in the covenant; it is still increasing, like a house in the building up, and shall still continue our rest for ever, like a house built up. It shall be built up for ever; for the everlasting habitations we hope for in the new Jerusalem are of this building. If mercy shall be built for ever, then the <hi type="italic">tabernacle of David, which has fallen down,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">be raised out of its ruins,</hi> and <hi type="italic">built up as in the days of old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Amos ix. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> mercy shall be built up for ever, because <hi type="italic">thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens.</hi> Though our expectations are in some particular instances disappointed, yet God's promises are not disannulled; they are <hi type="italic">established in the very heavens</hi> (that is, in his eternal counsels); they are above the changes of this lower region and out of the reach of the opposition of hell and earth. The stability of the material heavens is an emblem of the truth of God's word; the heavens may be clouded by vapours arising out of the earth, but they cannot be touched, they cannot be changed. (2.) An abstract of the covenant upon which this faith and hope are built: <hi type="italic">I have said it,</hi> says the psalmist, for <hi type="italic">God hath sworn it,</hi> that the heirs of promise might be entirely satisfied of the immutability of his counsel. He brings in God speaking (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.3">v. 3</reference>), owning, to the comfort of his people, "<hi type="italic">I have made a covenant,</hi> and therefore will make it good." The covenant is made with David; the covenant of royalty is made with him, as the father of his family, and with his seed through him and for his sake, representing the covenant of grace made with Christ as head of the church and with all believers as his spiritual seed. David is here called <hi type="italic">God's chosen</hi> and <hi type="italic">his servant;</hi> and, as God is not changeable to recede from his own choice, so he is not unrighteous to cast off one that served him. Two things encourage the psalmist to build his faith on this covenant:—[1.] The ratification of it; it was confirmed with an oath: <hi type="italic">The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent.</hi> [2.] The perpetuity of it; the blessings of the covenant were not only secured to David himself, but were entailed on his family; it was promised that his family should continue—<hi type="italic">Thy seed will I establish for ever,</hi> so that <hi type="italic">David shall not want a son to reign</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.20-Jer.33.21">Jer. xxxiii. 20, 21</reference>); and that it should continue a royal family—<hi type="italic">I will build up thy throne to all generations,</hi> to all the generations of time. This has its accomplishment only in Christ, of the seed of David, who lives for ever, to whom God has given the throne of his father David, and of the increase of whose government and peace there shall be no end. Of this covenant the psalmist will return to speak more largely, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">v. 19</reference>, &c.
entries.6cf09c7c1207ab577fd318a1b8e1cc1276169b5a: <div eID="gen12063" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Power and Justice; The Glory of God Celebrated.</title> <div sID="gen12064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And the heavens shall praise thy wonders, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : thy faithfulness also in the congregation of the saints. <hi type="super">6</hi> For who in the heaven can be compared unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="italic">who</hi> among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">7</hi> God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> about him. <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of hosts, who <hi type="italic">is</hi> a strong <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> like unto thee? or to thy faithfulness round about thee? <hi type="super">9</hi> Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces, as one that is slain; thou hast scattered thine enemies with thy strong arm. <hi type="super">11</hi> The heavens <hi type="italic">are</hi> thine, the earth also <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine: <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the world and the fulness thereof, thou hast founded them. <hi type="super">12</hi> The north and the south thou hast created them: Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in thy name. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou hast a mighty arm: strong is thy hand, <hi type="italic">and</hi> high is thy right hand. <hi type="super">14</hi> Justice and judgment <hi type="italic">are</hi> the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face. <div eID="gen12064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12065" type="x-p"/> These verses are full of the praises of God. Observe, <div eID="gen12065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12066" type="x-p"/> I. Where, and by whom, God is to be praised. 1. God is praised by the angels above: <hi type="italic">The heavens shall praise thy wonders, O Lord!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.5">v. 5</reference>; that is, "the glorious inhabitants of the upper world continually celebrate thy praises." <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, you his angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">Ps. ciii. 20</reference>. The works of God are wonders even to those that are best acquainted and most intimately conversant with them; the more God's works are known the more they are admired and praised. This should make us love heaven, and long to be there, that there we shall have nothing else to do but to praise God and his wonders. 2. God is praised by the assemblies of his saints on earth (<hi type="italic">praise waits for him in Zion</hi>); and, though their praises fall so far short of the praises of angels, yet God is pleased to take notice of them, and accept of them, and reckon himself honoured by them. "Thy faithfulness and the truth of thy promise, that rock on which the church is built, shall be praised in the congregation of the saints, who owe their all to that faithfulness, and whose constant comfort it is that there is a promise, and that he is faithful who has promised." It is expected from God's saints on earth that they praise him; who should, if they do not? Let every saint praise him, but especially the congregation of saints; when they come together, let them join in praising God. The more the better; it is the more like heaven. Of the honour done to God by the assembly of the saints he speaks again (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints.</hi> Saints should assemble for religious worship, that they may publicly own their relation to God and may stir up one another to give honour to him, and, in keeping up communion with God, may likewise maintain the communion of saints. In religious assemblies God has promised the presence of his grace, but we must also, in them, have an eye to his glorious presence, that the familiarity we are admitted to may not breed the least contempt; for he is terrible in his holy places, and therefore greatly to be feared. A holy awe of God must fall upon us, and fill us, in all our approaches to God, even in secret, to which something may very well be added by the solemnity of public assemblies. God must be had <hi type="italic">in reverence of all that are about him,</hi> that attend him continually as his servants or approach him upon any particular errand. See <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>. Those only serve God acceptably who serve him with <hi type="italic">reverence and godly fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">Heb. xii. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen12066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12067" type="x-p"/> II. What it is to praise God; it is to acknowledge him to be a being of unparalleled perfection, such a one that there is none like him, nor any to be compared with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">v. 6</reference>. If there be any beings that can pretend to vie with God, surely they must be found among the angels; but they are all infinitely short of him: <hi type="italic">Who in the heaven can be compared with the Lord,</hi> so as to challenge any share of the reverence and adoration which are due to him only, or to set up in rivalship with him for the homage of the children of men? They are sons of the mighty, but which of them can be likened unto the Lord? Nobles are princes' peers; some parity there is between them. But there is none between God and the angels; they are not his peers. <hi type="italic">To whom will you liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa. xl. 25</reference>. This is insisted on again (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is a strong Lord like unto thee?</hi> No angel, no earthly potentate, whatsoever, is comparable to God, or <hi type="italic">has an arm like him,</hi> or can <hi type="italic">thunder with a voice like him.</hi> Thy <hi type="italic">faithfulness is round about thee;</hi> that is, "thy angels who are round about thee, attending thee with their praises and ready to go on thy errands, are all faithful." Or, rather, "In every thing thou doest, on all sides, thou approvest thyself faithful to thy word, above whatever prince or potentate was." Among men it is too often found that those who are most able to break their word are least careful to keep it; but God is both strong and faithful; he can do every thing, and yet will never do an unjust thing. <div eID="gen12067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12068" type="x-p"/> III. What we ought, in our praises, to give God the glory of. Several things are here mentioned. 1. The command God has of the most ungovernable creatures (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou rulest the raging of the sea,</hi> than which nothing is more frightful or threatening, nor more out of the power of man to give check to; it can swell no higher, roll no further, beat no harder, continue no longer, nor do any more hurt, than God suffers it. "<hi type="italic">When the waves thereof arise</hi> thou canst immediately hush them asleep, still them, and make them quiet, and turn the storm into a calm." This coming in here as an act of omnipotence, what manner of man then was the Lord Jesus, whom the <hi type="italic">winds and seas obeyed?</hi> 2. The victories God has obtained over the enemies of his church. His ruling the raging of the sea and quelling its billows was an emblem of this (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast broken Rahab,</hi> many a <hi type="italic">proud enemy</hi> (so it signifies), Egypt in particular, which is sometimes called <hi type="italic">Rahab,</hi> broken it in pieces, as one that is slain and utterly unable to make head again. "The head being broken, thou hast scattered the remainder with the arm of thy strength." God has more ways than one to deal with his and his church's enemies. We think he should slay them immediately, but sometimes he scatters them, that he may send them abroad to be monuments of his justice, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">Ps. lix. 11</reference>. The remembrance of the breaking of Egypt in pieces is a comfort to the church, in reference to the present power of Babylon; for God is still the same. 3. The incontestable property he has in all the creatures of the upper and lower world (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.11-Ps.89.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): "Men are honoured for their large possessions; but <hi type="italic">the heavens are thine, O Lord! the earth also is thine;</hi> therefore we praise thee, therefore we trust in thee, therefore we will not fear what man can do against us. <hi type="italic">The world and the fulness thereof,</hi> all the riches contained in it, all the inhabitants of it, both the tenements and the tenants, are all thine; for <hi type="italic">thou hast founded them,</hi>" and the founder may justly claim to be the owner. He specifies, (1.) The remotest parts of the world, the north and south, the countries that lie under the two poles, which are uninhabited and little known: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast created them,</hi> and therefore knowest them, takest care of them, and hast tributes of praise from them." The north is said to be <hi type="italic">hung over the empty place;</hi> yet what fulness there is there God is the owner of it. (2.) The highest parts of the world. He mentions the two highest hills in Canaan—"<hi type="italic">Tabor and Hermon</hi>" (one lying to the west, the other to the east); "these shall rejoice in thy name, for they are under the care of thy providence, and they produce offerings for thy altar." The little hills are said to rejoice in their own fruitfulness, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.12">Ps. lxv. 12</reference>. Tabor is commonly supposed to be that high mountain in Galilee on the top of which Christ was transfigured; and then indeed it might be said to rejoice in that voice which was there heard, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> 4. The power and justice, the mercy and truth, with which he governs the world and rules in the affairs of the children of men, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.13-Ps.89.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. (1.) God is able to do every thing; for his is the Lord God Almighty. His arm, his hand, is mighty and strong, both to save his people and to destroy his and their enemies; none can either resist the force or bear the weight of his mighty hand. <hi type="italic">High is his right hand,</hi> to reach the highest, even those that <hi type="italic">set their nests among the stars</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.2-Amos.9.3">Amos ix. 2, 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Obad.1.4">Obad. 4</reference>); his <hi type="italic">right hand is exalted</hi> in what he has done, for in thousands of instances he has signalized his power, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.16">Ps. cxviii. 16</reference>. (2.) He never did, nor ever will do, any thing that is either unjust or unwise; for <hi type="italic">righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne.</hi> None of all his dictates or decrees ever varied from the rules of equity and wisdom, nor could ever any charge God with unrighteousness or folly. Justice and judgment are the <hi type="italic">preparing</hi> of his throne (so some), the <hi type="italic">establishment</hi> of it, so others. The preparations for his government in his counsels from eternity, and the establishment of it in its consequences to eternity, are all justice and judgment. (3.) He always does that which is kind to his people and consonant to the word which he has spoken: "<hi type="italic">Mercy and truth shall go before thy face,</hi> to prepare thy way, as harbingers to make room for thee—mercy in promising, truth in performing—truth in being as good as thy word, mercy in being better." How praiseworthy are these in great men, much more in the great God, in whom they are in perfection!
entries.4222f141fb733271c15c4a1cb4003f108b0c7717: <div eID="gen12068" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blessedness of Israel Declared.</title> <div sID="gen12069" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , in the light of thy countenance. <hi type="super">16</hi> In thy name shall they rejoice all the day: and in thy righteousness shall they be exalted. <hi type="super">17</hi> For thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the glory of their strength: and in thy favour our horn shall be exalted. <hi type="super">18</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> our defence; and the Holy One of Israel <hi type="italic">is</hi> our king. <div eID="gen12069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12070" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having largely shown the blessedness of the God of Israel, here shows the blessedness of the Israel of God. As <hi type="italic">there is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, so, happy art thou, O Israel! there is none like unto thee, O people!</hi> especially as a type of the gospel-Israel, consisting of all true believers, whose happiness is here described. <div eID="gen12070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12071" type="x-p"/> I. Glorious discoveries are made to them, and glad tidings of good brought to them; they hear, <hi type="italic">they know, the joyful sound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.15">v. 15</reference>. This may allude, 1. To the shout of a victorious army, the shout of a king, <reference osisRef="Num.23.21">Num. xxiii. 21</reference>. Israel have the tokens of God's presence with them in their wars; the sound of the <hi type="italic">going in the top of the mulberry-trees</hi> was indeed a <hi type="italic">joyful sound</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.24">2 Sam. v. 24</reference>); and they often returned making the earth ring with their songs of triumph; these were joyful sounds. Or, 2. To the sound that was made over the sacrifices and on the solemn feast-day, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.1-Ps.81.3">Ps. lxxxi. 1-3</reference>. This was the happiness of Israel, that they had among them the free and open profession of God's holy religion, and abundance of joy in their sacrifices. Or, 3. To the sound of the jubilee-trumpet; a joyful sound it was to servants and debtors, to whom it proclaimed release. The gospel is indeed a joyful sound, a sound of victory, of liberty, of communion with God, and the <hi type="italic">sound of abundance of rain;</hi> blessed are the people that hear it, and know it, and bid it welcome. <div eID="gen12071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12072" type="x-p"/> II. Special tokens of God's favour are granted them: "<hi type="italic">They shall walk, O Lord! in the light of thy countenance;</hi> they shall govern themselves by thy directions, shall be guided by the eye; and they shall delight themselves in thy consolations. They shall have the favour of God; they shall know that they have it, and it shall be continual matter of joy and rejoicing to them. They shall go through all the exercises of a holy life under the powerful influences of God's lovingkindness, which shall make their duty pleasant to them and make them sincere in it, aiming at this, as their end, to be accepted of the Lord." We then walk in the light of the Lord when we fetch all our comforts from God's favour and are very careful to keep ourselves in his love. <div eID="gen12072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12073" type="x-p"/> III. They never want matter for joy: Blessed are God's people, for in his name, in all that whereby he has made himself known, if it be not their own fault, <hi type="italic">they shall rejoice all the day.</hi> Those that rejoice in Christ Jesus, and make God their exceeding joy, have enough to counterbalance their grievances and silence their griefs; and therefore their joy is full (<reference osisRef="1John.1.4">1 John i. 4</reference>) and constant; it is their duty to rejoice evermore. <div eID="gen12073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12074" type="x-p"/> IV. Their relation to God is their honour and dignity. They are happy, for they are high. <hi type="italic">Surely in the Lord,</hi> in the Lord Christ, <hi type="italic">they have righteousness and strength,</hi> and so are recommended by him to the divine acceptance; and therefore <hi type="italic">in him shall all the seed of Israel glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24-Isa.45.25">Isa. xlv. 24, 25</reference>. So it is here, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.16-Ps.89.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. 1. "In <hi type="italic">thy righteousness shall they be exalted,</hi> and not in any righteousness of their own." We are exalted out of danger, and into honour, purely by the righteousness of Christ, which is a clothing both for dignity and for defence. 2. "Thou art the <hi type="italic">glory of their strength,</hi>" that is, "thou art their strength, and it is their glory that thou art so, and what they glory in." <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God who always causes us to triumph.</hi> 3. "In thy favour, which through Christ we hope for, <hi type="italic">our horn shall be exalted.</hi>" The horn denotes beauty, plenty, and power; these those have who are made accepted in the beloved. What greater preferment are men capable of in this world than to be God's favourites? <div eID="gen12074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12075" type="x-p"/> V. Their relation to God is their protection and safety (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For our shield is of the Lord</hi>" (so the margin) "and <hi type="italic">our king is from the Holy One of Israel.</hi> If God be our ruler, he will be our defender; and who is he then that can harm us?" It was the happiness of Israel that God himself had the erecting of their bulwarks and the nominating of their king (so some take it); or, rather, that he was himself a <hi type="italic">wall of fire round about them,</hi> and, as a Holy One, the author and centre of their holy religion; he was their King, and so their glory in the midst of them. Christ is the Holy One of Israel, that holy thing; and in nothing was that peculiar people more blessed than in this, that <hi type="italic">he</hi> was born King of the Jews. Now this account of the blessedness of God's Israel comes in here as that to which it was hard to reconcile their present calamitous state.
entries.237f6fba57df77d476a7d04ebac6ca96bb377c9d: <div eID="gen12075" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Covenant with David.</title> <div sID="gen12076" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Then thou spakest in vision to thy holy one, and saidst, I have laid help upon <hi type="italic">one that is</hi> mighty; I have exalted <hi type="italic">one</hi> chosen out of the people. <hi type="super">20</hi> I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: <hi type="super">21</hi> With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him. <hi type="super">22</hi> The enemy shall not exact upon him; nor the son of wickedness afflict him. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I will beat down his foes before his face, and plague them that hate him. <hi type="super">24</hi> But my faithfulness and my mercy <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> with him: and in my name shall his horn be exalted. <hi type="super">25</hi> I will set his hand also in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers. <hi type="super">26</hi> He shall cry unto me, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation. <hi type="super">27</hi> Also I will make him <hi type="italic">my</hi> firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. <hi type="super">28</hi> My mercy will I keep for him for evermore, and my covenant shall stand fast with him. <hi type="super">29</hi> His seed also will I make <hi type="italic">to endure</hi> for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven. <hi type="super">30</hi> If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments; <hi type="super">31</hi> If they break my statutes, and keep not my commandments; <hi type="super">32</hi> Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. <hi type="super">33</hi> Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. <hi type="super">34</hi> My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. <hi type="super">35</hi> Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David. <hi type="super">36</hi> His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me. <hi type="super">37</hi> It shall be established for ever as the moon, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> a faithful witness in heaven. Selah. <div eID="gen12076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12077" type="x-p"/> The covenant God made with David and his seed was mentioned before (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.3-Ps.89.4">v. 3, 4</reference>); but in these verses it is enlarged upon, and pleaded with God, for favour to the royal family, now almost sunk and ruined; yet certainly it looks at Christ, and has its accomplishment in him much more than in David; nay, some passages here are scarcely applicable at all to David, but must be understood of Christ only (who is therefore called <hi type="italic">David our king,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>), and very great and precious promises they are which are here made to the Redeemer, which are strong foundations for the faith and hope of the redeemed to build upon. The comforts of our redemption flow from the covenant of redemption; all our springs are in that, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Acts xiii. 34</reference>. Now here we have an account of those sure mercies. Observe, <div eID="gen12077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12078" type="x-p"/> I. What assurance we have of the truth of the promise, which may encourage us to build upon it. We are here told, 1. How it was spoken (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou didst speak in vision to thy Holy One.</hi> God's promise to David, which is especially referred to here, was spoken in vision to Nathan the prophet, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.17">2 Sam. vii. 12-17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when the <hi type="italic">Holy One of Israel was their king</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.18">v. 18</reference>), he appointed David to be his viceroy. But to all the prophets, those holy ones, he <hi type="italic">spoke in vision</hi> concerning Christ, and to him himself especially, who had lain in his bosom from eternity, and was made perfectly acquainted with the whole design of redemption, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. 2. How it was sworn to and ratified (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Once have I sworn by my holiness,</hi> that darling attribute. In swearing by his holiness, he swore by himself; for he will as soon cease to be as be otherwise than holy. His swearing once is enough; he needs not swear again, as David did (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.17">1 Sam. xx. 17</reference>); for his word and oath are two immutable things. As Christ was made a priest, so he was made a king, <hi type="italic">by an oath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.21">Heb. vii. 21</reference>); for his kingdom and priesthood are both unchangeable. <div eID="gen12078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12079" type="x-p"/> II. The choice made of the person to whom the promise is given, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.19-Ps.89.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. David was a king of God's own choosing, so is Christ, and therefore both are called <hi type="italic">God's kings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. David was mighty, a man of courage and fit for business; he was chosen out of the people, not out of the princes, but the shepherds. God found him out, exalted him, laid help upon him, and ordered Samuel to anoint him. But this is especially to be applied to Christ. 1. He is one that is mighty, every way qualified for the great work he was to undertake, <hi type="italic">able to save to the uttermost</hi>—mighty in strength, for he is the Son of God—mighty in love, for he is able experimentally to compassionate those that are tempted. He is <hi type="italic">the mighty God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa. ix. 6</reference>. 2. He is <hi type="italic">chosen out of the people,</hi> one of us, bone of our bone, that takes part with us of flesh and blood. Being ordained for men, he is taken from among men, that his terror might not make us afraid. 3. God has found him. He is a Saviour of God's own providing; for the salvation, from first to last, is purely the Lord's doing. <hi type="italic">He has found the ransom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.24">Job xxxiii. 24</reference>. We could never have found a person fit to undertake this great work, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.3-Rev.5.4">Rev. v. 3, 4</reference>. 4. God has <hi type="italic">laid help upon him,</hi> not only helped him, but treasured up help in him for us, laid it as a charge upon him to help fallen man up again, to help the chosen remnant to heaven. <hi type="italic">In me is thy help,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.13.9">Hos. xiii. 9</reference>. 5. He has exalted him, by constituting him the prophet, priest, and king of his church, clothing him with power, raising him from the dead, and setting him at his own right hand. Whom God chooses and uses he will exalt. 6. He has anointed him, has qualified him for his office, and so confirmed him in it, by giving him the Spirit, not by measure, but without measure, infinitely above his fellows. He is called <hi type="italic">Messiah,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Anointed.</hi> 7. In all this he designed him to be his own servant, for the accomplishing of his eternal purpose and the advancement of the interests of his kingdom among men. <div eID="gen12079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12080" type="x-p"/> III. The promises made to this chosen one, to David in the type and the Son of David in the antitype, in which not only gracious, but glorious things are spoken of him. <div eID="gen12080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12081" type="x-p"/> 1. With reference to himself, as king and God's servant: and what makes for him makes for all his loving subjects. It is here promised, (1.) That God would stand by him and strengthen him in his undertaking (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">With him my hand</hi> not only shall be, but <hi type="italic">shall be established,</hi> by promise, shall be so established that he shall by it be established and confirmed in all his offices, so that none of them shall be undermined and overthrown, though by the man of sin they shall all be usurped and fought against. Christ had a great deal of hard work to do and hard usage to go through; but he that gave him commission gave him forces sufficient for the execution of his commission: "<hi type="italic">My arm also shall strengthen him</hi> to break through and bear up under all his difficulties." No good work can miscarry in the hand of those whom God himself undertakes to strengthen. (2.) That he should be victorious over his enemies, that they should not encroach upon him (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">The son of wickedness shall not exact upon him,</hi> nor afflict him. He that at first broke the peace would set himself against him that undertook to make peace, and do what he could to blast his design: but he could only reach to bruise his heel; further he could not exact upon him nor afflict him. Christ became a surety for our debt, and thereby Satan and death thought to gain advantage against him; but he satisfied the demands of God's justice, and then they could not exact upon him. <hi type="italic">The prince of this world cometh, but he has nothing in me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.30">John xiv. 30</reference>. Nay, they not only shall not prevail against him, but they shall fall before him (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will bend down his foes before his face;</hi> the prince of this world shall be cast out, principalities and powers spoiled, and he shall be the death of death itself, and the destruction of the grave, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">Hos. xiii. 14</reference>. Some apply this to the ruin which God brought upon the Jewish nation, that persecuted Christ and put him to death. But all Christ's enemies, who hate him and will not have him to reign over them, shall be brought forth and slain before him, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.27">Luke xix. 27</reference>. (3.) That he should be the great trustee of the covenant between God and men, that God would be gracious and true to us (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">My faithfulness and my mercy shall be with him.</hi> They were with David; God continued merciful to him, and so approved himself faithful. They were with Christ; God made good all his promises to him. But that is not all; God's mercy to us, and his faithfulness to us, are with Christ; he is not only pleased with him, but with us in him; and it is in him that all the promises of God are yea and amen. So that if any poor sinners hope for benefit by the faithfulness and mercy of God, let them know it is with Christ; it is lodged in his hand, and to him they must apply for it (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">My mercy will I keep for him,</hi> to be disposed of by him, <hi type="italic">for evermore;</hi> in the channel of Christ's mediation all the streams of divine goodness will for ever run. Therefore it is <hi type="italic">the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> which we <hi type="italic">look for unto eternal life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.21">Jude 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.2">John xvii. 2</reference>. And, as the mercy of God flows to us through him, so the promise of God is, through him, firm to us: <hi type="italic">My covenant shall stand fast with him,</hi> both the covenant of redemption made with him and the covenant of grace made with us in him. The new covenant is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> always new, and firmly established, because it is lodged in the hands of a Mediator, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.6">Heb. viii. 6</reference>. The covenant stands fast, because it stands upon this basis. And this redounds to the everlasting honour of the Lord Jesus, that to him the great cause between God and man is entirely referred and the Father has committed all judgment to him, that <hi type="italic">all men might honour him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.22-John.5.23">John v. 22, 23</reference>); therefore it is here said, <hi type="italic">In my name shall his horn be exalted;</hi> this shall be his glory, that God's <hi type="italic">name is in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">Exod. xxiii. 21</reference>), and that he acts in God's name. <hi type="italic">As the Father gave me commandment, so I do.</hi> (4.) That his kingdom should be greatly enlarged (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will set his hand in the sea</hi> (he shall have the dominion of the seas, and the isles of the sea), and <hi type="italic">his right hand in the rivers,</hi> the inland countries that are watered with rivers. David's kingdom extended itself to the Great Sea, and the Red Sea, to the river of Egypt and the river Euphrates. But it is in the kingdom of the Messiah that this has its full accomplishment, and shall have more and more, when <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdoms of the Lord and of his Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev. xi. 15</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the isles shall wait for his law.</hi> (5.) That he should own God as his Father, and God would own him as his Son, his firstborn, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.26-Ps.89.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. This is a comment upon these words in Nathan's message concerning Solomon (for he also was a type of Christ as well as David), <hi type="italic">I will be his Father and he shall be my Son</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2 Sam. vii. 14</reference>), and the relation shall be owned on both sides. [1.] <hi type="italic">He shall cry unto me, Thou art my Father.</hi> It is probable that Solomon did so; but we are sure Christ did so, in the days of his flesh, when he offered up strong cries to God, and called him <hi type="italic">holy Father, righteous Father,</hi> and taught us to address ourselves to him as <hi type="italic">our Father in heaven.</hi> Christ, in his agony, cried unto God, <hi type="italic">Thou art my Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.39">Matt. xxvi. 39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.42">42</reference>, <hi type="italic">O my Father</hi>), and, upon the cross, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them; Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.</hi> He looked upon him likewise as his God, and therefore he perfectly obeyed him, and submitted to his will in his whole undertaking (he is <hi type="italic">my God and your God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>), and as the rock of his salvation, who would bear him up and bear him out in his undertaking, and make him more than a conqueror, even a complete Saviour; and therefore with an undaunted resolution he <hi type="italic">endured the cross, despising the shame,</hi> for he knew he should be both justified and glorified. [2.] <hi type="italic">I will make him my firstborn.</hi> I see not how this can be applied to David; it is Christ's prerogative to be <hi type="italic">the firstborn of every creature,</hi> and, as such, the <hi type="italic">heir of all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col. i. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.2 Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 2, 6</reference>. When <hi type="italic">all power was given to Christ both in heaven and in earth, and all things were delivered unto him by the Father,</hi> then god made him his firstborn, and far higher, more great and honourable, than the kings of the earth; for he is the King of kings, <hi type="italic">angels, authorities, and powers, being made subject to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Pet. iii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen12081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12082" type="x-p"/> 2. With reference to his seed. God's covenants always took in the seed of the covenanters; this does so (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">v. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.36">36</reference>): <hi type="italic">His seed shall endure for ever,</hi> and with it his throne. Now this will be differently understood according as we apply it to Christ or David. <div eID="gen12082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12083" type="x-p"/> (1.) If we apply it to David, by his seed we are to understand his successors, Solomon and the following kings of Judah, who descended from the loins of David. It is supposed that they might degenerate, and not walk in the spirit and steps of their father David; in such a case they must expect to come under divine rebukes, such as the house of David was at this time under, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.38">v. 38</reference>. But let this encourage them, that, though they were corrected, they should not be abandoned or disinherited. This refers to that part of Nathan's message (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14-2Sam.7.15">2 Sam. vii. 14, 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him,</hi> but <hi type="italic">my mercy shall not depart from him.</hi> Thus far David's seed and throne did endure for ever, that, notwithstanding the wickedness of many of his posterity, who were the scandals of his house, yet his family continued, and continued in the imperial dignity, a very long time,—that, as long as Judah continued a kingdom, David's posterity were kings of it, and the royalty of that kingdom was never in any other family, as that of the ten tribes was, in Jeroboam's first, then in Baasha's, &c.,—and that the family of David continued a family of distinction till that Son of David came whose throne should endure for ever; see <reference osisRef="Luke.1.27 Luke.1.32">Luke i. 27, 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.4 Luke.2.11">ii. 4, 11</reference>. If David's posterity, in after-times, should forsake God and their duty and revolt to the ways of sin, God would bring desolating judgments upon them and ruin the family; and yet he would not take away his lovingkindness from David, nor break his covenant with him; for, in the Messiah, who should come out of his loins, all these promises shall have their accomplishment to the full. Thus, when the Jews were rejected, the apostle shows that God's covenant with Abraham was not broken, because it was fulfilled in his spiritual seed, the heirs of the righteousness of faith, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom. xi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen12083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12084" type="x-p"/> (2.) If we apply it to Christ, by his seed we are to understand his subjects, all believers, his spiritual seed, the children which God has given him, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 13</reference>. This is that seed which shall be made to endure for ever, and his throne in the midst of them, in the church in the heart, <hi type="italic">as the days of heaven.</hi> To the end Christ shall have a people in the world to serve and honour him. <hi type="italic">He shall see his seed; he shall prolong his days.</hi> This holy seed shall endure for ever in a glorified state, when time and days shall be no more; and thus Christ's throne and kingdom shall be perpetuated: the kingdom of his grace shall continue through all the ages of time and the kingdom of his glory to the endless ages of eternity. <div eID="gen12084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12085" type="x-p"/> [1.] The continuance of Christ's kingdom is here made doubtful by the sins and afflictions of his subjects; their iniquities and calamities threaten the ruin of it. This case is here put, that we may not be offended when it comes to be a case in fact, but that we may reconcile it with the stability of the covenant and be assured of that notwithstanding. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is here supposed that there will be much amiss in the subjects of Christ's kingdom. His children may <hi type="italic">forsake God's law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.30">v. 30</reference>) by omissions, and <hi type="italic">break his statutes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.31">v. 31</reference>) by commissions. There are spots which are the spots of God's children, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.5">Deut. xxxii. 5</reference>. Many corruptions there are in the bowels of the church, as well as in the hearts of those who are the members of it, and these corruptions break out. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They are here told that they must smart for it (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will visit their transgression with a rod,</hi> their transgression sooner than that of others. <hi type="italic">You only have I known, and therefore I will punish you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. Their being related to Christ shall not excuse them from being called to an account. But observe what affliction is to God's people. 1. It is but a rod, not an axe, not a sword; it is for correction, not for destruction. This denotes gentleness in the affliction; it is the rod of men, such a rod as men use in correcting their children; and it denotes a design of good in and by the affliction, such a rod as yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness. 2. It is a rod on the hand of God <hi type="italic">(I will visit them</hi>), he who is wise, and knows what he does, gracious, and will do what is best. 3. It is a rod which they shall never feel the smart of but when there is great need: <hi type="italic">If they break my law, then I will visit their transgression with the rod,</hi> but not else. Then it is requisite that God's honour be vindicated, and that they be humbled and reduced. <div eID="gen12085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12086" type="x-p"/> [2.] The continuance of Christ's kingdom is made certain by the inviolable promise and oath of God, notwithstanding all this (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Nevertheless, my kindness will I not</hi> totally and finally <hi type="italic">take from him. First,</hi> "Notwithstanding their provocations, yet my covenant shall not be broken." Note, Afflictions are not only consistent with covenant-love, but to the people of God they flow from it. Though David's seed be chastened, it does not follow that they are disinherited; they may be cast down, but they are not cast off. God's favour is continued to his people, 1. For Christ's sake; in him the mercy is laid up for us, and God says, <hi type="italic">I will not take it from him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will not lie unto David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">v. 35</reference>. We are unworthy, but he is worthy. 2. For the covenant's sake: <hi type="italic">My faithfulness shall not fail, my covenant will I not break.</hi> It was supposed that they had broken God's statutes, <hi type="italic">profaned and polluted</hi> them (so the word signifies); "But," says God, "I will not break, I will not profane and pollute, my covenant;" it is the same word. That which is said and sworn is that God will have a church in the world as long as sun and moon endure, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.36-Ps.89.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. The sun and moon are faithful witnesses in heaven of the wisdom, power, and goodness of the Creator, and shall continue while time lasts, which they are the measurers of; but the <hi type="italic">seed of Christ shall be established for ever,</hi> as <hi type="italic">lights of the world</hi> while the world stands, to shine in it, and, when it is at an end, they shall be established lights shining in the firmament of the Father.
entries.1050ab03dc7dddf04880c70153daacf0a94326c2: <div eID="gen12086" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Expostulations; David's Expostulation with God.</title> <div sID="gen12087" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. <hi type="super">39</hi> Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown <hi type="italic">by casting it</hi> to the ground. <hi type="super">40</hi> Thou hast broken down all his hedges; thou hast brought his strong holds to ruin. <hi type="super">41</hi> All that pass by the way spoil him: he is a reproach to his neighbours. <hi type="super">42</hi> Thou hast set up the right hand of his adversaries; thou hast made all his enemies to rejoice. <hi type="super">43</hi> Thou hast also turned the edge of his sword, and hast not made him to stand in the battle. <hi type="super">44</hi> Thou hast made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground. <hi type="super">45</hi> The days of his youth hast thou shortened: thou hast covered him with shame. Selah. <hi type="super">46</hi> How long, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? wilt thou hide thyself for ever? shall thy wrath burn like fire? 47 Remember how short my time is: wherefore hast thou made all men in vain? <hi type="super">48</hi> What man <hi type="italic">is he that</hi> liveth, and shall not see death? shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave? Selah. <hi type="super">49</hi> Lord, where <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy former lovingkindnesses, <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou swarest unto David in thy truth? <hi type="super">50</hi> Remember, Lord, the reproach of thy servants; <hi type="italic">how</hi> I do bear in my bosom <hi type="italic">the reproach of</hi> all the mighty people; <hi type="super">51</hi> Wherewith thine enemies have reproached, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; wherewith they have reproached the footsteps of thine anointed. <hi type="super">52</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for evermore. Amen, and Amen. <div eID="gen12087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12088" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen12088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12089" type="x-p"/> I. A very melancholy complaint of the present deplorable state of David's family, which the psalmist thinks hard to be reconciled to the covenant God made with David. "Thou saidst thou wouldst not <hi type="italic">take away thy lovingkindness, but thou hast cast off.</hi>" Sometimes, it is no easy thing to reconcile God's providences with his promises, and yet we are sure they are reconcilable; for God's works fulfil his word and never contradict it. 1. David's house seemed to have lost its interest in God, which was the greatest strength and beauty of it. God had been pleased with his anointed, but now he was <hi type="italic">wroth with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.38">v. 38</reference>), had entered into covenant with the family, but now, for aught he could perceive, he had made void the covenant, not broken some of the articles of it, but cancelled it, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">v. 39</reference>. We misconstrue the rebukes of Providence if we think they make void the covenant. When the great anointed one, Christ himself, was upon the cross, God seemed to have cast him off, and was wroth with him, and yet did not make void his covenant with him, for that was established for ever. 2. The honour of the house of David was lost and laid in the dust: <hi type="italic">Thou hast profaned his crown</hi> (which was always looked upon as sacred) by <hi type="italic">casting it to the ground,</hi> to be trampled on, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">v. 39</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou hast made his glory to cease</hi> (so uncertain is all earthly glory, and so soon does it wither) and <hi type="italic">thou hast cast his throne down to the ground,</hi> not only dethroned the king, but put a period to the kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.44">v. 44</reference>. If it was penned in Rehoboam's time, it was true as to the greatest part of the kingdom, five parts of six; if in Zedekiah's time, it was more remarkably true of the poor remainder. Note, Thrones and crowns are tottering things, and are often laid in the dust; but there is a crown of glory reserved for Christ's spiritual seed which fadeth not away. 3. It was exposed and made a prey to all the neighbours, who insulted over that ancient and honourable family (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast broken down all his hedges</hi> (all those things that were a defence to them, and particularly that hedge of protection which they thought God's covenant and promise had made about them) and thou <hi type="italic">hast made even his strong-holds a ruin,</hi> so that they were rather a reproach to them than any shelter; and then, <hi type="italic">All that pass by the way spoil him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.41">v. 41</reference>) and make an easy prey of him; see <reference osisRef="Ps.80.12-Ps.80.13">Ps. lxxx. 12, 13</reference>. The enemies talk insolently: <hi type="italic">He is a reproach to his neighbours,</hi> who triumph in his fall from so great a degree of honour. Nay, every one helps forward the calamity (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.42">v. 42</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast set up the right hand of his adversaries,</hi> not only given them power, but inclined them to turn their power this way." If the enemies of the church lift up their hand against it, we must see God setting up their hand; for they could have <hi type="italic">no power unless it were given them from above.</hi> But, when God does permit them to do mischief to his church, it pleases them: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast made all his enemies to rejoice;</hi> and this is for thy glory, that those who hate thee should have the pleasure to see the tears and troubles of those that love thee." 4. It was disabled to help itself (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.43">v. 43</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast turned the edge of his sword,</hi> and made it blunt, that it cannot do execution as it has done; and (which is worse) thou hast turned the edge of his spirit, and taken off his courage, <hi type="italic">and hast not made him to stand</hi> as he used to do <hi type="italic">in the battle.</hi>" The spirit of men is what the Father and former of spirits makes them; nor can we stand with any strength or resolution further than God is pleased to uphold us. If men's hearts fail them, it is God that dispirits them; but it is sad with the church when those cannot stand who should stand up for it. 5. It was upon the brink of an inglorious exit (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.45">v. 45</reference>): <hi type="italic">The days of his youth hast thou shortened;</hi> it is ready to be cut off, like a young man in the flower of his age. This seems to intimate that the psalm was penned in Rehoboam's time, when the house of David was but in the days of its youth, and yet waxed old and began to decay already. Thus it was covered with shame, and it was turned very much to its reproach that a family which, in the first and second reign, looked so great, and made such a figure, should, in the third, dwindle and look so little as the house of David did in Rehoboam's time. But it may be applied to the captivity in Babylon, which, in comparison with what was expected, was but the day of the youth of that kingdom. However, the kings then had remarkably the <hi type="italic">days of their youth shortened,</hi> for it was in the days of their youth, when they were about thirty years old, that Jehoiachin and Zedekiah were carried captives to Babylon. <div eID="gen12089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12090" type="x-p"/> From all this complaint let us learn, 1. What work sin makes with families, noble royal families, with families in which religion has been uppermost; when posterity degenerates, it falls into disgrace, and iniquity stains their glory. 2. How apt we are to place the promised honour and happiness of the church in something external, and to think the promise fails, and the covenant is made void, if we be disappointed of that, a mistake which we now are inexcusable if we fall into, since our Master has so expressly told us that his kingdom is not of this world. <div eID="gen12090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12091" type="x-p"/> II. A very pathetic expostulation with God upon this. Four things they plead with God for mercy:— <div eID="gen12091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12092" type="x-p"/> 1. The long continuance of the trouble (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.46">v. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">How long, O Lord! wilt thou hide thyself? For ever?</hi> That which grieved them most was that God himself, as one displeased, did not appear to them by his prophets to comfort them, did not appear for them by his providences to deliver them, and that he had kept them long in the dark; it seemed an eternal night, when God had withdrawn: <hi type="italic">Thou hidest thyself for ever.</hi> Nay, God not only hid himself from them, but seemed to set himself against them: "<hi type="italic">Shall thy wrath burn like fire?</hi> How long shall it burn? Shall it never be put out? What is hell, but the wrath of God, burning for ever? And is that the lot of thy anointed?" <div eID="gen12092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12093" type="x-p"/> 2. The shortness of life, and the certainty of death: "Lord, let thy anger cease, and return thou, in mercy to us, remembering how short my time is and how sure the period of my time. Lord, since my life is so transitory, and will, ere long, be at an end, let it not be always so miserable that I should rather choose no being at all than such a being." Job pleads thus, <reference osisRef="Job.10.20-Job.10.21">ch. x. 20, 21</reference>. And probably the psalmist here urges it in the name of the house of David, and the present prince of that house, the <hi type="italic">days of whose youth</hi> were <hi type="italic">shortened,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.45">v. 45</reference>. <div eID="gen12093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12094" type="x-p"/> (1.) He pleads the shortness and vanity of life (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.47">v. 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">Remember how short my time is, how transitory I am</hi> (say some), therefore unable to bear the power of thy wrath, and therefore a proper object of thy pity. <hi type="italic">Wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Unto what vanity hast thou created all the sons of Adam!</hi> Now, this may be understood either, [1.] As declaring a great truth. If the ancient lovingkindnesses spoken of (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.49">v. 49</reference>) be forgotten (those relating to another life), man is indeed made in vain. Considering man as mortal, if there were not a future state on the other side of death, we might be ready to think that man was made in vain, and was in vain endued with the noble powers and faculties of reason and filled with such vast designs and desires; but God would not make man in vain; therefore, Lord, <hi type="italic">remember those lovingkindnesses.</hi> Or, [2.] As implying a strong temptation that the psalmist was in. It is certain <hi type="italic">God has not made all men,</hi> nor any man, <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">Isa. xlv. 18</reference>. For, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> If we think that God has made men in vain because so many have short lives, and long afflictions, in this world, it is true that God has made them so, but it is not true that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they are made in vain. For those whose days are few and full of trouble may yet glorify God and do some good, may keep their communion with God and get to heaven, and then they are not made in vain. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> If we think that God has made men in vain because the most of men neither serve him nor enjoy him, it is true that, as to themselves, they were made in vain, better for them had they not been born than not to be born again; but it was not owing to God that they were made in vain; it was owing to themselves; nor are they made in vain as to him, for he has <hi type="italic">made all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil,</hi> and those whom he is not glorified by he will be glorified upon. <div eID="gen12094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12095" type="x-p"/> (2.) He pleads the universality and unavoidableness of death (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.48">v. 48</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What man</hi>" (what <hi type="italic">strong man,</hi> so the word is) "<hi type="italic">is he that liveth and shall not see death?</hi> The king himself, of the house of David, is not exempted from the sentence, from the stroke. Lord, since he is under a fatal necessity of dying, let not his whole life be made thus miserable. <hi type="italic">Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave?</hi> No, he shall not when his time has come. Let him not therefore be delivered into the hand of the grave by the miseries of a dying life, till his time shall come." We must learn here that death is the end of all men; our eyes must shortly be closed to see death; there is no discharge from that war, nor will any bail be taken to save us from the prison of the grave. It concerns us therefore to make sure a happiness on the other side of death and the grave, that, <hi type="italic">when we fail, we may be received into everlasting habitations.</hi> <div eID="gen12095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12096" type="x-p"/> 3. The next plea is taken from the kindness God had for and the covenant he made with his servant David (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.49">v. 49</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, where are thy former lovingkindnesses,</hi> which thou showedst, nay, <hi type="italic">which thou swaredst, to David in thy truth?</hi> Wilt thou fail of doing what thou hast promised? Wilt thou undo what thou hast done? Art not thou still the same? Why then may not we have the benefit of the former sure mercies of David?" God's unchangeableness and faithfulness assure us that God will not cast off those whom he has chosen and covenanted with. <div eID="gen12096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12097" type="x-p"/> 4. The last plea is taken from the insolence of the enemies and the indignity done to God's anointed (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.50-Ps.89.51">v. 50, 51</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Remember, Lord, the reproach,</hi> and let it be rolled away from us and returned upon our enemies." (1.) They were God's servants that were reproached, and the abuses done to them reflected upon their master, especially since it was for serving him that they were reproached. (2.) The reproach cast upon God's servants was a very grievous burden to all that were concerned for the honour of God: "<hi type="italic">I bear in my bosom the reproach of all the mighty people,</hi> and am even overwhelmed with it; it is what I lay much to heart and can scarcely keep up my spirits under the weight of." (3.) "They are thy enemies who do thus reproach us; and wilt thou not appear against them as such?" (4.) <hi type="italic">They have reproached the footsteps of thy anointed.</hi> They reflected upon all the steps which the king had taken in the course of his administration, tracked him in all his motions, that they might make invidious remarks upon every thing he had said and done. Or, if we may apply it to Christ, the Lord's Messiah, they reproached the Jews with his footsteps, the slowness of his coming. They have reproached the delays of the Messiah; so Dr. Hammond. They called him, <hi type="italic">He that should come;</hi> but, because he had not yet come, because he did not now come to deliver them out of the hands of their enemies, when they had none to deliver them, they told them he would never come, they must give over looking for him. The scoffers of the latter days do, in like manner, reproach the footsteps of the Messiah when they ask, <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3-2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 3, 4</reference>. The reproaching of the footsteps of the anointed some refer to the serpent's <hi type="italic">bruising the heel of the seed of the woman,</hi> or to the sufferings of Christ's followers, who tread in his footsteps, and are reproached for his name's sake. <div eID="gen12097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12098" type="x-p"/> III. The psalm concludes with praise, even after this sad complaint (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.52">v. 52</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord for evermore, Amen, and amen.</hi> Thus he confronts the reproaches of his enemies. The more others blaspheme God the more we should bless him. Thus he corrects his own complaints, chiding himself for quarrelling with God's providences and questioning his promises; let both these sinful passions be silenced with the praises of God. However it be, yet God is good, and we will never think hardly of him; God is true, and we will never distrust him. Though the glory of David's house be stained and sullied, this shall be our comfort, that God is blessed for ever, and his glory cannot be eclipsed. If we would have the comfort of the stability of God's promise, we must give him the praise of it; in blessing God, we encourage ourselves. Here is a double <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> according to the double signification. <hi type="italic">Amen—so it is,</hi> God is blessed for ever. <hi type="italic">Amen—be it so,</hi> let God be blessed for ever. He began the psalm with thanksgiving, before he made his complaint (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.1">v. 1</reference>); and now he concludes it with a doxology. Those who give God thanks for what he has done may give him thanks also for what he will do; God will follow those with his mercies who, in a right manner, follow him with their praises.  <chapter eID="Ps.89"/> <div eID="gen12098" type="x-p"/>

entries.3dd4fb3513c443c5c8aadb2103263df6d3683f0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6526"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 89</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52">Psa 89:1-52</reference>. Of Ethan--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.88.1">Psa 88:1</reference>, title). This Psalm was composed during some season of great national distress, perhaps Absalom's rebellion. It contrasts the promised prosperity and perpetuity of David's throne (with reference to the great promise of <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.17">2Sa 7:12-17</reference>), with a time when God appeared to have forgotten His covenant. The picture thus drawn may typify the promises and the adversities of Christ's kingdom, and the terms of confiding appeal to God provided appropriate prayers for the divine aid and promised blessing.</title> <div sID="gen10000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6526"/><hi type="bold">1. mercies--</hi>those promised (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Ac 13:34</reference>), and--<div eID="gen10000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faithfulness--</hi>that is, in fulfilling them. <div eID="gen10001" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a0969f3b9a5d8f6db19f86b3a275712334ffb6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6527"/><div sID="gen10002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6527"/><hi type="bold">2. I have said--</hi>expressed, as well as felt, my convictions (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">2Co 4:13</reference>). <div eID="gen10002" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca39b71ccbde72639e082625b3376f4de487705b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6528"/><div sID="gen10003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6528"/>3-4. The object of this faith expressed in God's words (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.11-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:11-16</reference>).<div eID="gen10003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>or literally, "to"<div eID="gen10004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my chosen--</hi>as the covenant is in the form of a promise. <div eID="gen10005" type="x-p"/>
entries.6332908e5075da7fe03a2b2a1fe3945eeeea2220: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6529"/><div sID="gen10006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6529"/>6-7. This is worthy of our belief, for His faithfulness (is praised) by the congregation of saints or holy ones; that is, angels (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">De 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Da 8:13</reference>).<div eID="gen10006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sons of the mighty--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1">Psa 29:1</reference>). So is He to be admired on earth. <div eID="gen10007" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7e4e92a42876149d9cf64b93fad97870375df53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6530"/><div sID="gen10008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6530"/>8-14. To illustrate His power and faithfulness examples are cited from history. His control of the sea (the most mighty and unstable object in nature), and of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Psa 87:4</reference>), the first great foe of Israel (subjected to utter helplessness from pride and insolence), are specimens. At the same time, the whole frame of nature founded and sustained by Him, Tabor and Hermon for "east and west," and "north and south," together representing the whole world, declare the same truth as to His attributes. <div eID="gen10008" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d75780b386b832628c2481ca3923ef70e9a6d75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6532"/><div sID="gen10010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6532"/>15. His government of righteousness is served by "mercy" and "truth" as ministers (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.10-Ps.85.13">Psa 85:10-13</reference>).<div eID="gen10010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know the joyful sound--</hi>understand and appreciate the spiritual blessings symbolized by the feasts to which the people were called by the trumpet (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Le 25:9</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen10011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walk ... countenance--</hi>live in His favor (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">44:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10012" type="x-p"/>
entries.746b54dcd75d5fe8b02dab190962348b10bfe450: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6533"/><div sID="gen10013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6533"/><hi type="bold">16-17. in--</hi>or, "by"<div eID="gen10013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy righteousness--</hi>Thy faithful just rule.<div eID="gen10014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>or, "beauty."<div eID="gen10015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of their strength--</hi>They shall be adorned as well as protected.<div eID="gen10016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our horn--</hi>exalt our power (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">Psa 75:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Lu 1:69</reference>). <div eID="gen10017" type="x-p"/>
entries.37e1be6799977b2a349b6cbc0dce6c64dabd5cb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6534"/><div sID="gen10018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6534"/>18. (Margin). Thus is introduced the promise to "our shield," "our king," David. <div eID="gen10018" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fd3b64f62dd6c68171d5836136291ebcda9053a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6535"/><div sID="gen10019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6535"/><hi type="bold">19-37. Then--</hi>when the covenant was established, of whose execution the exalted views of God now given furnish assurance.<div eID="gen10019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou ... to thy holy one--</hi>or godly saint, object of favor (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>). Nathan is meant (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.17">2Sa 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.3-1Chr.17.15">1Ch 17:3-15</reference>).<div eID="gen10020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid help--</hi>literally, "given help." David was chosen and then exalted. <div eID="gen10021" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b7682e15ddf1fb6d95c8e01962d2d9f6505650e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6544"/><div sID="gen10033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6544"/>38-52. present a striking contrast to these glowing promises, in mournful evidences of a loss of God's favor.<div eID="gen10033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast off--</hi>and rejected (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.15.4">Psa 15:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">43:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.9">44:9</reference>). <div eID="gen10034" type="x-p"/>

entries.278067507549b70aaf9994518e994db533964414: <div eID="gen21517" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21520" type="x-p"/> The psalmist shows God's great mercy to the house of David, and the promises which he had given to it of support and perpetuity, vv. 1-37; complains that, notwithstanding these promises, the kingdom of Judah is overthrown, and the royal family nearly ruined, <reference osisRef="Psa.89.38-Psa.89.45">Psa 89:38-45</reference>; and earnestly prays for their restoration, <reference osisRef="Psa.89.46-Psa.89.52">Psa 89:46-52</reference>. <div eID="gen21520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21521" type="x-p"/> It is most probable that this Psalm was composed during the captivity. Of Ethan and Heman we have already seen something in the introduction to the preceding Psalm; see also the parallel places in the margin. The title should probably be translated, - To give instruction to Ethan the Ezrahite. The Chaldee has, "A good instruction, delivered by Abraham, who came from the east country." The Septuagint and Ethiopic have Nathan the Israelite; the Arabic has Nathan the Israelite. <div eID="gen21521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21522" type="x-p"/> The Psalm divides itself into two grand parts; the first extends, verses 1-37, in which the psalmist shows God's mercy to the house of David, and the promises which he has given to it of support and perpetuity. The second part begins with <reference osisRef="Psa.89.38">Psa 89:38</reference>, and ends with the Psalm; and in it the author complains that notwithstanding these promises, the kingdom of Judah is overthrown and the royal family ruined; and he entreats the Lord to remember his covenant made with that family, and restore them from their captivity. <div eID="gen21522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21523" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21524" type="x-p"/> I will sing of the mercies of the Lord - I will celebrate the mercy of God to the house of Jacob; the mercy that has been shown to our fathers from time immemorial. <div eID="gen21524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21525" type="x-p"/> To all generations - What I say concerning thy mercy and goodness, being inspired by thy Spirit, is not only true, but shall be preserved by the Divine providence for ever.
entries.927a16ce0583cab1fe05c93bc35ff19c8f835c86: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21526" type="x-p"/> Mercy shall be built up for ever - God's goodness is the foundation on which his mercy rests; and from that source, and on that foundation, acts of mercy shall flow and be built up for ever and ever. <div eID="gen21526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21527" type="x-p"/> Thy faithfulness shalt thou establish - What thou hast promised to do to the children of men on earth, thou dost register in heaven, and thy promise shall never fail.
